paras: The threatened lynching of Ed Hall took place near Charlotte, North Carolina, in late July 1905, when about a hundred men hunted Hall, a young Black man accused of attempting to assault a farmer's wife, and there was talk of lynching him. He was arrested at Pineville the same afternoon and jailed, the talk subsided, and in August he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to seven years at hard labor.

Hall worked in Charlotte as a driver at Auten's meat market and was sent to the Auten farm home, about four miles outside the city, to fetch meat. The wire story placed the house four miles southeast of Charlotte in one printing and four miles east on the Dilworth road in another.

According to the Charlotte special, Hall was "half drunk" and, at about 9:30 in the morning, seized Mrs. Mack Auten from behind while she telephoned for him and tried to drag her into another room. Her screams brought a Mr. Beatty, who was working nearby, and Hall ran; the story said she was found half fainting with torn clothes and bruises.

Hall eluded "a hundred men on his trail" until 4 p.m., when he was arrested at Pineville and "safely landed in jail" in Charlotte. The same report said there had been "some talk of lynching" that morning, but that it had quieted down and the authorities expected no trouble.

On August 17 Hall pleaded guilty in the Superior Court at Charlotte, in a hearing that a Raleigh paper said lasted about ten minutes, long enough for Mrs. Auten to testify, and did not go to a jury. Judge C. M. Cooke sentenced him to seven years at hard labor in the state prison, saying this was the limit of the law and, given Hall's age, a just punishment.

Coverage came entirely from white newspapers, and no report in the Black press was found. The Wilmington Semi-weekly Messenger reprinted the Raleigh Post's Charlotte special on August 1 under the headline "BRUTE HUNTED DOWN", called the alleged attack an "outrage", and mentioned the lynching talk without comment. South Carolina's Keowee Courier ran the same text a day later as "Negro Attempts Rape in Charlotte", datelined July 26, but left out the manhunt and the lynching talk.

The sentence was reported in Charlotte specials to the Raleigh News and Observer and the Richmond Times-Dispatch on August 18, and in a Washington Evening Star news brief on August 21. These reports still described Hall as "the negro who attempted a criminal assault", while the Evening Star spelled the woman's name "Austin" and placed the sentencing on a Friday.

The date is uncertain in the coverage: the Messenger's undated reprint appeared August 1, while the Courier's dateline gives July 26 and the Times-Dispatch called the assault "a few weeks" before August 17.

framing.detail: The Messenger's reprint ran under 'BRUTE HUNTED DOWN' and 'Woman's Cries Brought Help in Her Hour of Peril', called the alleged act 'The outrage', and reported the lynching talk without criticism.
The Keowee Courier ran the same text as 'Negro Attempts Rape in Charlotte' and dropped the passage about the manhunt and lynching talk.
The sentencing reports ('A SEVEN YEAR SENTENCE', 'Negro Given Seven Years') gave the court result briefly, still describing Hall as 'the negro who attempted a criminal assault'.
